Artificial Intelligence.summary: Sudden cardiac death mostly originates from post-infarct ventricular tachycardia. This reentry is sustained by propagation around scar tissue, but its risk remains difficult to predict from infarct imaging alone. While in silico induction studies can reveal these mechanisms, exploring many substrates and pacing locations remains computationally expensive. We propose a graph attention classifier for early prediction of sustained ventricular reentry from simulated cardiac electrophysiology. Each simulation is represented as a graph with early nodal voltage samples and edge attributes encoding geometry, stimulation frequency, tissue labels, amplitude, and diastolic interval. These descriptors are computed only from the first two paced activations, before sustained reentry is observed. On a balanced independent test set of 1000 simulations, the classifier achieves 94.6% accuracy, 95.4% sensitivity, 93.8% specificity, 94.6% F1-score, 0.987 ROC-AUC, and 0.985 PR-AUC. Ablation experiments show that diastolic interval is the most critical descriptor. Qualitative attention inspection suggests that different heads focus on border-zone, stimulation location, and early propagation path. These results support graph attention as a fast early-prediction approach for large-scale in silico ventricular reentry studies.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Living Context Graphs: Continual Semantic Learning for Enterprise Data Reasoning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Enterprise AI can now perform analytics, reporting, and data-driven workflows, yet the data foundations it relies on remain hard to operationalize: business meaning, relationships, metric definitions, and reporting conventions are absent from database schemas and scattered across undocumented systems and tribal knowledge. We introduce the Living Context Graph (LCG), a continually learned context layer that makes existing enterprise data operational for AI without requiring a copy or transformation of the underlying warehouse. LCG bootstraps base semantics and relationships from the data itself, builds a concept graph that indexes business context as queries are served, writes durable semantic learnings from verified outcomes, and withdraws or re-earns context when later outcomes contradict prior routes. We evaluate LCG through text-to-SQL, a core data-reasoning task, on a transfer-aware split of three BIRD databases comprising 499 questions: 353 form the learning history and 146 are held out and never used to update the context layer. Bootstrapping alone improves overall accuracy by +4.6 percentage points. Learning only from the history raises accuracy on the untouched held-out transfer set by +22.6 points (95% CI [+14.4, +30.8]), exceeding five-shot retrieval from the same history by +12.3 points. Incremental learning reaches the one-shot endpoint within observed evaluation noise on every database. Ablating the graph changes held-out accuracy by at most one question per database but increases per-query cost 2.3-3.3x and median latency 1.8-3.4x: continually learned semantics drive accuracy, while the graph makes that context efficient to serve.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 22 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Continual Learning in the Era of Foundation Models and Embodied Agents. Data splits and annotations: https://github.com/varunagrawal2002/Living-Context-Graph

Artificial Intelligence.title: Hilbert States for Decision-Making under Partial Observability
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Decision-making under partial observability can be fundamentally limited by information, even with known dynamics: distinct physical states can induce the same observation history while favoring different actions. We study three questions: when is full-state optimality unattainable, what information exactly preserves the best observation-based decision, and how does finite-data learning affect reliability? First, we characterize decision ambiguity through conditional action preferences. We give a zero-regret criterion, a positive lower bound for conflicting uniquely optimal actions on positive-probability regions with uniformly positive cost gaps, and an exact binary-action regret formula. This also shows why physical-state ambiguity alone need not cause decision loss. Second, for two actions and squared terminal-goal costs in the plane, we derive an exact inner-product representation of conditional expected cost differences using three conditional moment contrasts and a goal-dependent feature. This Hilbert state preserves observation-optimal actions without hidden-state reconstruction. Under nondegenerate history and goal variation, its three-dimensional form is minimal among exact bilinear cost-contrast representations. Third, we relate finite-data state errors to excess decision regret via goal-projected errors, action margins, and goal geometry. Physics-based simulations verify information-limited regret, exact action preservation, and the role of second moments. Held-out real-SAR experiments demonstrate feasible goal-conditioned decisions from masked images, while finite-data evaluations reveal goal-dependent reliability. Together, these results separate irreducible information loss, exact representation sufficiency, and learning-induced excess regret.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Jev-as-a-Reward: Validating Probabilistic Safety Judges for Reinforcement Learning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Probabilistic safety judges return the probability of a safety label and cheaply score reinforcement learning rollouts. A confidence gate sends only uncertain verdicts to a stronger LLM judge, which leaves confidently passed harm in a blind spot. Policies can exploit this blind spot, and commercial judges release new versions. We propose a protocol that validates such a judge before and during training, separates the share of confidently passed harm from its amount, and re-validates it after each judge change. We apply it to two versions of Jev, a commercial decision-only judge, and to an open guard classifier. Under the probability reward of Jev, passed harm shrinks in all 11 runs under the primary reference, mostly more slowly than caught harm, and concentrates in the blind spot. Binarizing this judge meets the escape criterion on Llama, and the open guard classifier shows an escape signal in one seed under a second reference. Guard classifiers share this blind spot, and even frontier LLM judges catch at most one of 10 human-labeled confident misses. Without a trained reward model, the probability reward with a helpfulness term lowers HarmBench attack success on Llama-3.1-8B from 0.287 to at most 0.033 at the final checkpoint.

Artificial Intelligence.title: vividRGB: Various visual cue detection in RGB photographs with forced focused attention
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Natural photographs contain dense, overlapping structures that can be weakly expressed in feature maps from whole-image vision encoders. We introduce forced focused attention (FFA) and its Python implementation, vividRGB. FFA is an encoder-agnostic inference-time procedure that applies a frozen encoder to enlarged, overlapping local crops, averages inverse-aligned reflections, and reconstructs a feature field in source coordinates. We evaluate 50 high-resolution photographs from grassland vegetation, fungal networks, airborne forests, coral reefs, and phytoplankton microscopy, using DINOv3 ViT-B/16. Across the five domains, FFA at 5% or 10% focus produces higher mean RGB-edge boundary F1 than direct DINOv3 encoding and automatic SAM3 masks. Domain means range from 0.244 to 0.596 for FFA, versus 0.028-0.076 for direct DINOv3 and 0.020-0.090 for SAM3. Qualitative feature maps also show finer appearance structure. These results concern RGB-edge preservation rather than verified species, traits, or biological segmentation. Narrower focus generally improves boundary preservation, while extraction time and GPU energy use increase sharply and gains diminish at finer settings. FFA may be useful for relatively small, high-resolution ecological image collections where dense visual cues matter. The alpha release vividRGB 0.1.0 and versioned research resources support reproducible cue inspection.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 32 pages including supplementary material; 6 numbered figures and a graphical summary

Artificial Intelligence.title: ReA-Bench: Benchmarking Responsible Agent Auditing
Artificial Intelligence.summary:
As agents perform tasks autonomously in local and cloud environments, auditing their execution trajectories can help service providers identify risks and improve agent harnesses and foundation models. Our analysis of production and red-team trajectories shows that some risks are repeatedly missed across auditing configurations. Overall recall obscures which risks are missed and whether higher recall comes with more false positives on legitimate behavior. Existing benchmarks offer limited insight into these failures. Generated trajectories can contain inconsistent tool calls and responses, conspicuous risky actions, or repetitive attack patterns. Grouping results by risk type also makes it difficult to tell whether auditors overlooked evidence, accepted an unsupported conclusion, or lacked information needed to make a judgment.
  We introduce ReA-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark for auditing responsible agent behavior. It organizes auditing challenges into six tiers: internal safety knowledge, contradictions within trajectories, evidence retrieval in long contexts, verification of sources and reasoning, indirect steering, and missing information. It includes challenging benign cases in which actions resemble risky ones but are consistent with the task and its authorization. It also provides paired trajectory versions to test whether auditors detect the same risks more reliably when the trajectory is shortened or missing information is supplied. Most samples are drawn from real production trajectories, with scenarios manually selected and adapted to preserve realistic tasks and risks that could plausibly arise during execution.

Artificial Intelligence.title: ReAccess: Look Once, Stay Focused with Efficient Test Time Memory
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Despite recent advances, vision-language models (VLMs) still struggle with fine-grained visual understanding, often failing to effectively utilize critical evidence already encoded in their visual representations. Existing approaches address this limitation through repeated visual processing or explicit reasoning, introducing substantial computational overhead. In this paper, we propose ReAccess, a lightweight framework that preserves and reuses question-relevant visual evidence through compact associative memory. Constructed during a single visual prefill, the memory supports progressive evidence retrieval that steers both attention queries and hidden representations, enabling effective visual grounding without repeated image encoding or explicit reasoning traces. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in both general visual understanding and fine-grained perception, while achieving substantially faster inference than existing reasoning-intensive approaches, demonstrating a promising path to efficient multimodal reasoning.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Razavi-Bench: Tracking AI Progress in Analog Circuit Reasoning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: We propose Razavi-Bench, a benchmark built from the 50 questions in Razavi's two Analog Design Experiments With AI articles and graded by GPT-6 Luna against reference answers and rubrics, and use it to track how fast AI models improve at analog circuit analysis. Across 73 multimodal large language models released between May 2024 and November 2026, the top score rose from 28.83% to 98.33% in 30 months, mostly before the reference answers were published. The leading models now answer almost every textbook question correctly; the hardest questions show a circuit that resembles a textbook one but works differently, or ask about behavior the obvious analysis misses. Within two and a half years, a set of questions that exposed the limits of AI models has become one they answer almost perfectly.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Project page: https://razavi-bench.tokenzhang.com ; code and data: https://github.com/Arcadia-1/razavi-bench

Artificial Intelligence.title: Advancing Cognitive Pairwise Comparisons for Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence and Data Science: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Human-centric artificial intelligence and data science (HCAD) systems increasingly involve human-in-the-loop (HITL) interventions to overcome the limitations of fully automated machine learning algorithms, such as automation bias and the inability to incorporate tacit domain knowledge, and continuously improve predictive performance. Data transformations, feature selection, feature weighting, and model selection usually require laborious human involvement across iterations of artificial intelligence and data science (AI&DS) pipelines, making development a challenging and time-consuming process. The Cognitive Pairwise Comparison (CPC) framework is proposed as a human-centric methodology to elicit preferences and priorities in a structured format. To establish essential facets of human-centricity, this research advances the CPC methodology so that user preference elicitation can be systematically quantified in these challenging AI&DS tasks. To demonstrate the usability and validity of these facets, this study presents several applications within movie recommender systems using the MovieLens dataset. It exemplifies how the extended CPC framework can facilitate interactions between human judgments and data across supervised learning, dimensionality reduction, and unsupervised learning algorithms.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 33 pages, 19 tables, 8 figures; interactive web demos available at https://kkfyuen.github.io/cpcHCADDemos ; source code and datasets at https://github.com/kkfyuen/cpcHCADDemos ; archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23434993 ; earlier preprint version available at SSRN 4048692 (http://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4048692 or https://ssrn.com/abstract=4048692)

Artificial Intelligence.title: Experience Rot: Experienced Agents Fail Where Novices Succeed
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Agents are increasingly built to learn from experience: they keep conversation histories, memory files, retrieved notes and skills, and reuse what worked before. We show that this experience turns against them when their tools change silently. We test a range of models with tools defined as in the Model Context Protocol (MCP). After a silent change, experienced agents fail on most tasks, while agents new to the task mostly succeed. We call this failure Experience Rot. Experienced agents copy their earlier call instead of checking the current interface, even when the tool definition shows the change. Then they report success. When the documentation is incomplete, experience is what makes agents succeed. After a change, the same experience leaves them worse off than no experience at all. The failure appears in every form of memory we test and grows with the amount of experience. Simple remedies fall short: announcing the update barely helps, and pointing the agent to the documentation fails whenever the documentation does not spell out the answer.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Multi-LLM Agentic AI at the Edge: Joint Agent Scheduling and Resource Allocation
Artificial Intelligence.summary: In this paper, an edge-enabled multi-large language model (LLM) agentic AI architecture is proposed, where one supervisor AI agent and multiple worker AI agents cooperatively execute users' requests at the edge. The supervisor AI agent decouples the user request into a series of sub-tasks and dynamically dispatches them to LLM-equipped worker AI agents via two agentic workflows, i.e., parallel and serial workflows, with a two-level retry mechanism to enhance execution reliability. To prolong the service duration of worker AI agents, the energy minimization problems are formulated by jointly considering AI agent selection and resource allocation, subject to task execution latency and quality of service (QoS) constraints. A resource allocation scheme based on alternating optimization (AO) is proposed. Specifically, for the parallel workflow, the scheme decouples the original problem into bandwidth allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems, which are iteratively solved by the proposed successive convex approximation (SCA), Lagrangian relaxation (LR), and Gale-Shapley (GS) or LLM-based algorithms, respectively. For the serial workflow, the problem is similarly decoupled into service time allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems; the optimal service time allocation is obtained via Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, while the latter two sub-problems are addressed by extending the proposed algorithms to the serial scenario. Simulation results show that the proposed resource allocation scheme can reduce system energy consumption compared with other benchmarks, while experiments on a multi-LLM agentic AI system based on Qwen and Llama demonstrate improved task execution success rates.

Artificial Intelligence.title: LLM-as-a-Tutor: Policy-Aware Prompt Adaptation for Non-Verifiable RL
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) for non-verifiable instruction following increasingly relies on LLM judges with prompt-specific rubrics as reward signals. While recent methods adapt these rubrics to the evolving policy during training, the training prompts themselves remain static, drawn from fixed corpora. This static approach often results in a critical misalignment between prompt difficulty and policy capability, leaving the judge unable to recover a discriminative reward signal when prompts fail to elicit quality variance among rollouts. To address this misalignment, we introduce LLM-as-a-Tutor, a framework that extends the LLM's role from judge to tutor: a single model serves as an examiner that pairwise-compares policy rollouts to detect non-challenging prompts, and as a generator that appends atomic constraints to them. This append-only design preserves the original prompt while adding constraints to increase difficulty in step with the policy's capability, producing a self-calibrating training signal without external difficulty schedules. On three complex instruction-following benchmarks, our method outperforms both policy-unaware baselines and prior policy-adaptive methods that adapt rubrics or rewrite prompts, on average and on four of five metrics, suggesting prompt adaptation as an underexplored axis of policy-awareness in non-verifiable RL for constraint-heavy instruction following.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Analog Resonant Recurrent Neural Networks via Metacircuits
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Physical neural networks offer a promising route to fast and energy-efficient edge intelligence by embedding computation in the intrinsic dynamics of materials and devices. However, processing temporal signals requires recurrent networks with memory, whose trained dynamics are hard to reproduce faithfully in physical systems. Here we present an analog resonant recurrent neural network (R$^2$NN) implemented as a metacircuit of coupled local resonators. A reformulated mechanical-electrical analogy based on frequency-dependent negative resistances maps a trained network one-to-one onto the metacircuit, with every trainable parameter realized as a resistance. Training tunes local resonances and global resistive couplings so that past responses persist as recurrent memory and interfere with incoming inputs, and the resulting impedance landscape routes different frequencies to distinct outputs. Exploiting this recurrent memory, the metacircuit solves a temporal-parity task whose output depends on the entire input history. Building on the learned frequency selectivity, stand-alone R$^2$NN systems classify raw tactile, acoustic and vibration signals in real time and directly drive downstream hardware. This work establishes engineered locally resonant dynamics as a physical substrate for recurrent neural computation and opens a route to compact, low-latency neural hardware for machine intelligence at the edge.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: This version corresponds to the revised manuscript submitted for peer review on 10 November 2026. An earlier version was posted as arXiv:2604.17277v1 on 19 April 2026

Artificial Intelligence.title: PatentAgentBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents with Professional Patent Task Suites
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Patent practice lies at the intersection of technical, legal, and linguistic work, making it challenging yet crucial to technological innovation. Recently, rapid advances in large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems have demonstrated the potential to complete realistic business workflows and even patent works. This raises a question: can current AI systems perform patent work reliably? Existing benchmarks cover a limited range of patent tasks and simplify evidence acquisition by providing reference materials or candidate documents. In this paper, we introduce PatentAgentBench, a benchmark comprising 510 instances across eight task suites: novelty search, freedom-to-operate (FTO) search, design FTO, invalidity search, claim charting, patent drafting, office-action response, and patent translation. Curated from real patent records and professional materials, the benchmark combines task-specific metrics with expert-reviewed annotations and rubrics. Retrieval tasks such novelty search, FTO, etc., require agents to search and compare patent collections without a supplied candidate pool. The drafting and OAR tasks assess the quality of agents' work given technical disclosure and office action notice. We evaluate seven LLMs across four agent harnesses on PatentAgentBench, finding that current systems still struggle to identify novelty, assess risk, and understand practitioner intent throughout patent workflows.

Artificial Intelligence.title: A Survey of Data Agents: Emerging Paradigm or Overstated Hype?
Artificial Intelligence.summary: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has spurred the emergence of data agents, autonomous systems designed to orchestrate Data + AI ecosystems for tackling complex data-related tasks. However, the term "data agent" currently suffers from terminological ambiguity and inconsistent adoption, conflating simple query responders with sophisticated autonomous architectures. This terminological ambiguity fosters mismatched user expectations, accountability challenges, and barriers to industry growth. Inspired by the SAE J3016 standard for driving automation, this survey introduces the first systematic hierarchical taxonomy for data agents, comprising six levels that delineate and trace progressive shifts in autonomy, from manual operations (L0) to a vision of generative, fully autonomous data agents (L5), thereby clarifying capability boundaries and responsibility allocation. Through this lens, we offer a structured review of existing research arranged by increasing autonomy, encompassing specialized data agents for data management, preparation, and analysis, alongside emerging efforts toward versatile, comprehensive systems with enhanced autonomy. We further analyze critical evolutionary leaps and technical gaps for advancing data agents, especially the ongoing L2-to-L3 transition, where data agents evolve from procedural execution to autonomous orchestration. Finally, we conclude with a forward-looking roadmap, envisioning proactive, generative data agents. A curated companion repository is available at https://github.com/HKUSTDial/awesome-data-agents.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Please refer to our paper list and companion materials at: https://github.com/HKUSTDial/awesome-data-agents

Artificial Intelligence.title: Auditing a Moving Target: Evidence Anchoring and the Expiry of Fairness Audits of Provider-Served Language Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Organizations increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for decisions about people, such as hiring, investment and employee evaluation, and rely on them over long periods of time. Fairness audits of such systems, however, are conducted only once. We examine how the biases of LLMs change over time. In a venture screening setting, models from five providers decided whether and how much to invest in startups whose founders differed only in gender, origin and university. We repeated this audit three times over 13 months (248,400 API calls). Study 1 shows that the same model, called under the same identifier one year later, displayed a significantly different bias pattern. Study 2 shows that the successors of retired models carried the same bias as their predecessors, but in a significantly different size and form. Study 3 shows that the bias does not depend on the industry of the startup. A document analysis further shows that providers change and retire models at their discretion, with notice periods of zero to six months. Drawing on these findings, we develop a theory of evidence anchoring. We theorize that bias resides in the model class and persists, whereas audit evidence is anchored to a single model and expires when the provider decides. We derive policy advice for organizations and regulators, namely audits of model classes instead of single models, a version record for every model response, and re-audits triggered by model changes.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Analysis of Inverse Relation Directionality in Large Language Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance on text-to-knowledge graph generation and related tasks. Nevertheless, it is still unclear whether they accurately model the direction-dependent semantics of inverse relations, in which reversing the order of the arguments alters the meaning of a relation (e.g., \textit{mother} versus \textit{child}). To the best of our knowledge, this work presents the first systematic study of inverse relation directionality in LLMs, using a benchmark consisting of 5,457 instances spanning 27 distinct inverse relation labels. We evaluate five open-source LLMs under a multiple-choice prompting framework and further examine the influence of relation descriptions and entity representations by substituting the original entities with synthetic and masked entities. Our findings reveal systematic asymmetries in inverse relation classification across LLMs, indicate that relation descriptions do not consistently improve performance, and show that model performance can be sensitive to variations in entity representations.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Which AI Use Cases Deserve a Pilot? A Risk and Value Framework for Funding, Scoping, and Scaling AI
Artificial Intelligence.summary: A composite score can rank AI use cases while leaving the permitted operating scope and the evidence required for expansion unspecified. We treat the unit of decision as a use case at a proposed scope (authority, human mediation, limits, volume, environment, population) and define three decisions: screen the scope, fund the experiment, and authorize expansion only when residual risk is acceptable and evidence of incremental net value applies at that scope. A risk track (R1-R4) is implemented as an explicit decision table with vetoes and documented precedence, and a value track follows four evidence stages with each transition needing its own evidence. Funding uses expected value of perfect information as an upper bound and the value of sample information for the specific experiment. A quantified expected-loss check, required where policy says so, computes the containment an expansion needs and credits a control only on evidence measured at the proposed scope; in a synthetic scenario the highest-value control design fails that test while a smaller scope passes. A reproducible Python package with 279 passing tests demonstrates the framework on synthetic refund, reconciliation and knowledge-assistant use cases, including a synthetic matched-scope fixture and a transferability stress test (value evidence is simulated, not realized), and compares it with a public AWS sample. Thresholds and appetite are prototype policy requiring field validation.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 18 pages. All results use synthetic data. A companion Python package reproduces the tables

Artificial Intelligence.title: From Recursion to Convolution: Parallel Self-Improvement for Multi-Agent Systems
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Multi-agent self-improvement enables agents to improve through interaction and feedback. However, sequential dependencies across agents and refinement rounds can propagate errors, increase computational costs, and limit parallelism. Moreover, refining individual features or agents in isolation can overlook their dependencies and restrict collective coordination. To address these challenges, we propose ConvRSI, a framework for parallelizing multi-agent self-improvement through convolution. ConvRSI couples intra-agent convolution, which jointly refines related agent features, with inter-agent graph convolution, which aggregates messages according to the collaboration topology. Both stages operate in latent space, enabling parallel updates without repeatedly decoding and re-encoding intermediate messages. Experiments on MATH-500 show that ConvRSI achieves 5.04% performance improvement while reducing 17.27% inference cost, and 45.11% latency compared with RecursiveMAS. It also supports diverse collaboration patterns by representing their topologies as adjacency matrices. These results demonstrate the potential of convolutional co-evolution for efficient multi-agent self-improvement. Our code and datasets are provided in https://github.com/LYA2333/ConvRSI.

Artificial Intelligence.title: When the Editing Intent Is Split: A Cross-Modal Jailbreak Attack for Large Image Editing Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large image editing models increasingly infer editing intent from both textual and visual inputs, creating an underexplored safety risk when harmful intent is distributed across modalities. In this work, we formalize this split-intent vulnerability and propose the Split-Intent Jailbreak Attack (SIJA), which asymmetrically distributes an unsafe editing intent by specifying the editing referent in text while concealing the safety-critical action and specification through graphical visual semantics in an auxiliary cue. To systematically study this threat, we introduce the Split-Intent Image Editing Safety Benchmark (SI2ESBench) for evaluating image editing models under split-intent inputs. Extensive experiments on representative commercial and open-source models demonstrate that SIJA effectively compromises state-of-the-art image editing systems, achieving ASRs of 68.28% on GPT Image 2 and 91.38% on Qwen-Image-3.0-Pro. Our results expose a mismatch between multimodal editing and safety assessment: the distributed intent can be recovered to execute the requested transformation, yet its harmfulness often remains undetected by existing safeguards. To mitigate this vulnerability, we propose editing-intent reconstruction, a defense principle that explicitly evaluates the complete transformation implied by the joint multimodal context and substantially improves rejection of split-intent attacks. Our findings expose a cross-modal safety gap in modern image editing systems and highlight the need to assess the jointly inferred transformation rather than individual inputs in isolation. Project page: https://github.com/yexianmin/SIJA.

Artificial Intelligence.title: ARCANA: A Benchmark for Abstraction and Analogical Reasoning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Analogical reasoning is widely considered a fundamental component of human intelligence. Few benchmarks are designed to explicitly test far analogical reasoning - reasoning between domains that are superficially dissimilar yet share deep relational or structural similarities. In this work, we introduce an analogical reasoning benchmark called Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus of ANAlogy (ARCANA). The tasks of ARCANA require performing far analogical mappings from real-world objects or physical phenomena to abstract grid-based transformations, different from the well-known ARC-AGI benchmark which primarily emphasized innate human priors. We validate ARCANA through a human study, demonstrating that humans solve these tasks reliably. In contrast, evaluations across a range of large language models show a distinct performance gap compared to humans, revealing systematic failure modes that remain challenging for current models. To address this gap, we propose ConceptSIR, a reasoning framework based on concept slippage, introspection, and reflection. Experiments demonstrate that ConceptSIR enables standard LLMs to solve several challenging ARCANA tasks that were unsolved by direct prompting in our evaluation. Overall, our results suggest that far analogical reasoning remains an open problem for contemporary LLMs. All the materials are available at sites.google.com/view/arcanacogtest. The complete codebase, including benchmark, and ConceptSIR, is publicly available at https://github.com/density-11/arcana-test. All ARCANA data and task instances can be accessed and explored at https://arcanacogtest.org/.

Computational Engineering.title: What Does CLIP Learn for Regional Geolocalization? Probing Visual Cues and Scene Configuration After Adaptation
Computational Engineering.summary: Large collections of street-view imagery provide rich visual information about urban environments, but extracting fine-grained geographic information from such data remains challenging. In particular, fine-grained regional geolocalization is challenging because nearby areas often share coarse geographic cues. We study regional geolocalization within a metropolitan area and ask whether pretrained CLIP features are sufficient for regional discrimination, and what visual information supports performance after adaptation. Using 9,085 street-view images from eight Greater Los Angeles regions, we compare zero-shot CLIP, frozen-encoder readouts, partial encoder updating, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), and full fine-tuning. Frozen readouts remain near the 39.03% zero-shot accuracy, whereas encoder adaptation achieves 75.94-82.10%. Full fine-tuning also reduces the mean distance to the predicted region center from 12.30 km to 3.86 km. We probe these gains through semantic cue removal, appearance reduction using edge maps and blur, and scene-configuration disruption using patch scrambling. Adapted models achieve higher edge and blur accuracy and switch 42.92-45.56% of predictions after scrambling, compared with 10.79-14.60% for frozen methods. However, adaptation does not improve the fraction of performance retained after appearance reduction, while vegetation and sky remain influential. A Caltech101 control further shows that scrambling sensitivity is not unique to geolocalization. Overall, encoder adaptation substantially improves nearby-region discrimination and is associated with greater sensitivity to intact scene configuration, without evidence that coarse structure alone becomes sufficient for prediction. These conclusions concern viewpoint variation near known locations rather than geographically disjoint generalization.
Computational Engineering.comment: Accepted at IEEE BigData 2026

Computational Engineering.title: FLAT: Smoothing the Rugged Landscape for Learnable, Sample-Efficient Traffic Calibration
Computational Engineering.summary: Calibrating microscopic traffic models for urban digital twins is an expensive black-box optimization problem: evaluating each set of car-following and lane-changing parameters requires a full simulation, limiting the evaluations available per recalibration window. Matching raw trajectories yields a rugged objective that sparse surrogates struggle to learn, reducing sequential acquisition to near-random probing. We present FLAT, which couples what to optimize with where to sample next. An eight-dimensional behavioral fingerprint smooths the parameter-error landscape, making the objective learnable from a few dozen samples; annealed lower-confidence-bound (LCB) acquisition then spends each remaining run where it most reduces error. The LCB loop supports a Gaussian process (GP), random forest (RF), or multi-layer-perceptron (MLP) ensemble. Across six heterogeneous real-world scenes, FLAT-GP achieves the lowest scene-averaged behavioral error, winning 6/6 scenes against SPSA, GA, and CMA-ES and 5/6 against TPE under the matched 100-run budget. Some baselines require up to 4.4 times as many simulations to match. Ablations show objective choice shifts final behavioral error by 80.6% on average, removing sequential LCB raises the six-scene mean by 21.7%, and surrogate choice shifts it by at most 4.2%, confirming gains trace to objective geometry and sequential allocation rather than surrogate capacity.
Computational Engineering.comment: 9 pages, 28 figures. Code and cache: https://github.com/QianyHP/FLAT-calibration

Computational Engineering.title: PointZip: Statistically Lossless Compression for Climate Data with Pointwise Error Bounds
Computational Engineering.summary: High-resolution climate simulations generate data volumes that increasingly strain storage, I/O, and data dissemination. Error-bounded lossy compressors can reduce these costs, but their tolerances are usually user-chosen and difficult to standardize across heterogeneous climate datasets. We address this limitation with statistically lossless compression, where the pointwise compression error is bounded by the pointwise data uncertainty. We propose PointZip, a two-stage compressor that combines a rate-distortion-efficient base layer with error-bound-aware residual coding to enforce pointwise guarantees. On outputs from the widely used climate modeling framework ICON, PointZip makes 1km simulations practical by reducing storage bandwidth requirements by 72x. On the ERA5 climate dataset, PointZip reaches 69.3x on the most representative variables, reducing the commonly used subset to 4 TB. In downstream evaluations, PointZip preserves data spectra, extreme events, and air parcel trajectories, while increasing neural weather forecast RMSE by less than 1%, with negligible impact on the Fractions Skill Score (FSS).
Computational Engineering.comment: 12 pages, 11 figures

Computational Engineering.title: Scientific Coding with Large Language Models: Evidence from Finite Element Analysis
Computational Engineering.summary: Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential route to automating scientific programming, but their usefulness depends on consistently producing numerically correct code. We extend FEM-Bench to 17 finite element tasks involving nonlinear and history-dependent mechanics and structural dynamics, and evaluate 15 models on implementation and test generation without execution feedback. The best model succeeds in 87.1% of single-pass implementation trials, but rankings differ between tracks. The leading implementer achieves 49.9% joint test success, while the leading tester reaches 82.6%. For six models, we compare single-pass generation with two agentic harnesses that allow code execution and revision. Agentic execution solves some tasks that never succeeded in single-pass trials and improves consistency on others, but gains vary across models and harnesses, and regressions also occur. Claude Opus 5 with SimpleAgent reaches 96.5% Pass@3, the probability of at least one success in three attempts, but 77.1% Pass$^3$, the probability that all three succeed. No model-harness combination exceeds 78.8% Pass$^3$. To understand why agents submit incorrect code after passing their own checks, we analyze 249 failed agentic trajectories and identify six categories of self-verification failure. The most common are inadequate test coverage (73.1%) and reliance on generic consistency checks (70.3%), and in 28.5% of cases the tests share an error with the implementation. Motivated by these findings, an exploratory configuration with separate coder and tester agents achieves the highest observed scores, with 97.6% Pass@3 and 88.8% Pass$^3$. These results identify consistency across attempts and independent verification as the main obstacles to trusting LLM-generated scientific code.
Computational Engineering.comment: 28 pages, 7 figures, 14 tables

Computational Engineering.title: A Hierarchically Compressed Immittance Operator Formulation for Fast Statics-to-Full-Wave Electromagnetic Simulation with the Boundary Element Method
Computational Engineering.summary: The boundary element method allows the electromagnetic simulation of three-dimensional problems with a two-dimensional discretization, using a surface integral representation of Maxwell's equations. For applications involving broadband simulations or multiscale geometries, the well-known low-frequency breakdown of conventional integral equation formulations must be addressed, while ensuring that dielectric, semiconducting, and lossy metallic regions are modeled rigorously, including the skin effect. In this work, a new boundary element formulation based on an immittance operator is proposed, where the underlying integral equations are inherently valid from statics to the full-wave regime. To enable efficient matrix assembly and solution, a hierarchical matrix compression strategy is devised, leveraging fast direct factorization as an intermediate step, and fast matrix-vector products for the iterative solution of the final system of equations. The proposed formulation is capable of electrostatic, magnetostatic, quasistatic, and full-wave simulations of dielectrics, semiconductors, and lossy metals. Representative numerical examples drawn from a variety of applications demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method.
Computational Engineering.comment: 15 pages, 12 figures. Submitted to the IEEE Transactions on Antennas and Propagation

Computational Engineering.title: The Walls Have Ears: Unveiling Cross-Chain Sandwich Attacks in DeFi
Computational Engineering.summary:
Cross-chain interoperability is a core component of modern blockchain infrastructure, enabling seamless asset transfers and composable applications across multiple blockchain ecosystems. However, the transparency of cross-chain messages can inadvertently expose sensitive transaction information, creating opportunities for adversaries to exploit value through manipulation or front-running strategies.
  In this work, we investigate cross-chain sandwich attacks targeting liquidity pool-based cross-chain bridge protocols. We uncover a critical vulnerability where attackers can exploit events emitted on the source chain to learn transaction details on the destination chain before they appear in the destination chain mempool. This information advantage allows attackers to strategically place front-running and back-running transactions, ensuring that their front-running transactions always precede those of existing MEV bots monitoring the mempool of the destination chain. Moreover, current sandwich-attack defenses are ineffective against this new cross-chain variant. To quantify this threat, we conduct an empirical study using cross-chain transaction data from the Symbiosis protocol (November 21, 2022 to April 4, 2026) and Debridge (December 21, 2022 to April 4, 2026), along with a tailored heuristic detection model. Our analysis indicates that this attack has indeed had a significant impact on DeFi.

Computational Engineering.title: A Neural Physics Solver for Richards Equation
Computational Engineering.summary: A new approach to discretise and solve Richards equation based on the finite element method (FEM) is presented. The novelty of the approach, called the Neural Physics method, is that it expresses the discretisation as a convolution neural network (CNN) whose weights are predetermined by the integrals of the basis functions in the FEM. The Neural Physics method is physically consistent as it represents a discretisation of the governing equation and can run on CPUs, GPUs and the latest AI accelerators, resulting in an increase in computational speed. The Neural Physics method is demonstrated for two different discretisations of Richards equation, including a multigrid method that is realised through a U-Net architecture. The accuracy and speed of these methods is tested on a problem with a known analytical solution and compared to a standard FEM, and shows that the Neural Physics method is almost an order of magnitude faster than a comparable FEM. Finally, the Neural Physics method is applied to a real-world test case with integrated experimental data and simulates the infiltration of water through a rain garden. This new approach therefore provides a route to efficiently and accurately solve Richards equation for a wide array of hydrological applications.
Computational Engineering.comment: 36 pages (including appendix), 7 figures, 3 tables

Computational Engineering.title: Multilayer Dual-polarized Microstrip Antenna Design by Topology Optimization with Enhanced Bandwidth
Computational Engineering.summary: Dual-polarized (DP) microstrip antennas are utilized in wireless systems for efficient data transmission. However, their bandwidth is typically very limited. In this contribution, we propose to design DP microstrip antennas with enhanced bandwidth using a density-based topology optimization approach. We formulate an optimization problem that simultaneously accounts for feeding port matching, the ports' isolation, and far-field dual-polarized performance. To enhance the bandwidth, we employ an FR4 stack-up, in which the copper on two layers is optimized simultaneously. We present two antenna designs operating around 5.7 GHz, which show a compromise in performance between a high isolation (more than 40 dB) and enhanced impedance bandwidth (around 10%). The optimized designs are experimentally validated, showing an excellent agreement between the simulated and measured performance.
Computational Engineering.comment: This work has been submitted for possible publication

Computational Engineering.title: Scaled boundary finite elements for FFT-based computational micromechanics
Computational Engineering.summary: We introduce a matrix-free FFT-based solver for three-dimensional linear elastic homogenization problems discretized by the scaled boundary finite element method (SBFEM) on a voxel grid. Owing to its analytical solution in the radial direction, the SBFEM discretization is inherently softer than fully integrated voxel finite elements, whereas its displacement-based formulation remains symmetric, conforming, and supports arbitrary stiffness anisotropy. These properties make SBFEM an attractive candidate for porous and highly heterogeneous microstructures, where existing voxel-based FFT discretizations offer no generally reliable choice: Reduced-integration hexahedral elements, equivalently the rotated staggered grid discretization, may suffer from hourglass instabilities in the presence of voids, whereas fully integrated hexahedral elements are often too stiff. The proposed discretization uses hexahedral SBFEM cells on the full voxel mesh of a regular periodic grid, retaining the simplicity of a fixed-resolution voxel representation without requiring adaptive mesh coarsening. The main contribution is a preconditioner based on the homogeneous SBFEM stiffness operator. We show that this preconditioner may be applied locally in Fourier space and that the condition number of the preconditioned system is bounded by the material contrast, independently of the grid resolution. This result enables a fully matrix-free implementation of the SBFEM-discretized problem, without assembling or storing the global stiffness matrix. Numerical experiments on a short-fibre reinforced composite, a polyurethane foam and a sand-based binder jet microstructure demonstrate robust convergence and competitive accuracy compared with established voxel discretizations. In particular, SBFEM remains stable for porous microstructures, for which reduced-integration hexahedral elements become unstable.
Computational Engineering.comment: 32 pages, 7 figures. Submitted to International Journal of Numerical Methods in Engineering

Computational Engineering.title: Newton-PINet: A fast physics-informed neural network with Newton linearization for meta-learning nonlinear PDEs
Computational Engineering.summary: Scientific machine learning has opened new avenues for solving parameterized partial differential equations (PDEs), enabling models to learn a family of PDEs and generalize to unseen instances. In this context, data-driven operator learning methods typically require large training datasets, while physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) suffer from difficult optimization and limited generalization, especially for nonlinear PDEs. We propose Newton-PINet, a physics-informed network enhanced by Newton linearization, offering an effective meta-learning framework for nonlinear PDEs. Newton-PINet (i) employs a physics-informed multilayer network with skip connections, where the output-layer weights are solved by least squares; (ii) adopts a two-stage learning strategy that first leverages gradient-based training to learn robust representations from the available training tasks, and then performs gradient-free fine-tuning on the output layer for fast task-specific generalization; and (iii) incorporates a Newton linearization method to speed up the least-squares iteration for nonlinear PDE problems. On a challenging nonlinear reaction-diffusion benchmark, Newton-PINet achieves up to three orders of magnitude lower relative error than recent neural solvers, while using 16x fewer training tasks and over an order of magnitude less training time (about 5 minutes versus several hours). This work advances the meta-learning of PINNs toward data-efficient, fast, and generalizable physics solvers. The code and datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/fycAIwj/Newton-PINet.
Computational Engineering.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026

Computational Engineering.title: Separating learning from search and feedback in budgeted inverse design of periodic unit cells
Computational Engineering.summary: To design a periodic material, engineers choose the shape and dimensions of a repeating cell to meet target properties. With few simulations, the benefit of a learned predictor can be hard to separate from the effect of which designs the search tries and how it uses simulator feedback. We compare two ways to predict properties in a library of 80 cell architectures, with up to 30 simulator calls per target. For each architecture, both searches use a table of predicted properties at different dimensions. One fills the table with predictions from neural networks. The other fits a simple model to the existing simulations for that architecture. Both searches use the difference between the predicted and simulated properties to adjust the next design. We generated 200 targets from simulated designs after fixing the analysis plan. The two searches showed no detectable difference in how often they matched all three properties within 2% or in the mean error of their returned designs. The upper limit of the 95% confidence interval for the gain in overall success rate was 4.5 percentage points. Follow-up controls on these targets changed success from 83.5% to 36.0% with a degraded table and 96.5% with an oracle table. In separate tests, using the simulation result to adjust the next design increased success for both types of table. Results cover one library and a coarse 32^3 voxel simulator. Designers can use this comparison to judge what a learned predictor adds when the search, feedback and budget are the same.
Computational Engineering.comment: 49 pages, 11 figures, including Supplementary Information

Computational Engineering.title: From Prediction to Action: An Execution-Aware End-to-End Machine Learning Framework for Structured Investment Decision Support
Computational Engineering.summary: Financial machine learning is widely used for market prediction, but many existing studies formulate trading as a directional forecasting problem and stop at predicting whether prices will rise or fall. Such predictions are difficult to translate directly into practical trading decisions, which also require execution rules, risk controls, and clearly defined actions. To address this gap, we propose an end-to-end machine learning framework for structured investment decision support. The framework integrates multi-asset market data, execution-aware label construction, feature engineering and refinement, specialist predictive models, and ensemble learning. Rather than defining learning targets solely according to future price direction, the proposed execution-aware formulation considers realised trading outcomes under predefined stop-loss and take-profit rules. Model outputs are subsequently converted into structured trading recommendations comprising trade direction, entry price, stop-loss, take-profit, and risk-reward ratio. The framework is evaluated using time-aware forward testing, with results showing that execution-aware labelling improves risk-adjusted trading performance over conventional directional labelling and that the integrated framework outperforms a simpler single-model baseline across key trading metrics. An automated cloud-based implementation further demonstrates the operational feasibility of the proposed approach. Overall, the findings suggest that closer alignment between predictive modelling, execution logic, and structured decision generation can improve the practical value of machine learning for financial trading.
Computational Engineering.comment: 26 pages, 5 figures

Computational Engineering.title: SLED: Sensor SLicing from Edge to Datacenter
Computational Engineering.summary: Modern sensing systems generate large volumes of heterogeneous data streams from multiple sensor modalities, increasing reliance on datacenters for computation, artificial intelligence/superintelligence (AI/SI) inference, and AI/SI training. Each sensor stream may have different network and compute requirements depending on its type and data volume. However, current wireless systems typically allocate resources at the device level, leading to contention among co-located sensor streams, where bulk data transfers may starve latency-critical telemetry. To this end, this paper introduces Sensor Slicing (SL). SL provides deterministic, medium access control (MAC)-level isolation for individual sensors within a single user equipment (UE) in open radio access networks (O-RAN). Using agentic coding techniques, SL is implemented in two O-RAN-compliant packages, reducing development time by 400 times (2 h 40 min [OCUDU] vs. 6.5 weeks [OAI]), 228-fold fewer human prompts (4 vs. 913), and less than half the tokens (0.64B vs. 1.43B). An associated end-to-end framework, SLED, is implemented to establish per-sensor radio and network isolation across edge, campus, and remote high-performance computing (HPC) tiers. Over-the-air wireless experiments demonstrate that while conventional network slicing causes critical delays to increase more than 2,300-fold under high traffic load, SLED maintains stable latency. Scaling evaluations on the two RAN stacks show that throughput remains within 0.9% and 1.4% of expected allocations even as the number of sensor slices increases. The results demonstrate that SLED preserves latency-critical telemetry while effectively utilizing resources across the sensor-to-HPC pipeline. The SLED software and evaluation datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/UNL-CPN-Lab/SLED-Sensor-SLicing-from-Edge-to-Datacenter.
Computational Engineering.comment: Accepted in IEEE Annual Congress on Artificial Intelligence of Things (IEEE AIoT) 2026. The SLED software and evaluation datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/UNL-CPN-Lab/SLED-Sensor-SLicing-from-Edge-to-Datacenter

Computational Engineering.title: Bookkeeping Is Not Judgement: EJBench, an Engineering Judgement Benchmark Built from a Conjugate Heat Transfer Design Campaign
Computational Engineering.summary: We introduce EJBench, a benchmark of engineering judgement: whether a model can predict how a design behaves at new conditions from a few earlier results, and decide on it. Unlike engineering benchmarks that test whether an agent can operate simulation or CAD software, EJBench is software-agnostic and asks what an engineer would conclude without running a simulation. Its tasks come from a conjugate heat transfer design campaign for battery cold plates, in three families: matching unlabelled test results to their operating points, choosing which stored runs to reveal before signing off a design, and ranking new duties by peak cell temperature. Every answer is taken from a converged simulation, not from an LLM judge. The best of ten frontier models, GPT-6 Astra, scores 0.71, and models state almost the same confidence on tasks they get wrong as on tasks they get right. We also post-train Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA and reinforcement learning, rewarded by the share of answer criteria the simulation results confirm; on the held-out test split its score rises from 0.071 to 0.106. We release the train, validation and test splits, the evaluation harness and the leaderboard.
Computational Engineering.comment: 23 pages

Computational Engineering.title: Solving the Discretised Shallow Water Equations on Distorted Structured Grids with Neural Physics
Computational Engineering.summary:
This paper presents a method for solving the shallow water equations on highly distorted structured grids using convolution-based operators following the Neural Physics approach. By mapping distorted physical grids to a uniform computational domain with Jacobian transformations, the governing advection and diffusion operators are reformulated in a structured convolutional form. This enables the use of efficient stencil-based operations and, following the Neural Physics concept, we do this through convolutional layers whose weights are determined by the chosen numerical methods rather than by training.
  The method introduces consistent mass-lumped formulations, conservative and non-conservative advection forms, and a diffusion operator, all expressed as convolutions. A nonlinear Petrov-Galerkin stabilisation is incorporated to control numerical oscillations on distorted meshes. Two approximations for the Laplacian operator are also proposed to accelerate pressure and diffusion solves. The framework is validated using the Carlisle 2005 flood event, demonstrating accurate predictions of water depth and velocity on distorted meshes for both linear and quadratic discretisations.
  The results show that distorted structured grids can retain conservation, stability and accuracy, whilst adapting the mesh statically. The convolutional formulation makes the method well suited to Neural Physics implementations and GPU acceleration, offering a scalable approach for flood modelling and large-scale geophysical simulations.
Computational Engineering.comment: 43 pages, 12 figures, 2 tables

Computational Engineering.title: ISLA: A Coordinate-Free, Measure-Weighted Transformer for Boundary-Driven PDEs
Computational Engineering.summary: Symmetry is a foundational principle of physics: the behavior of a PDE-governed system does not depend on the coordinate frame, unit system, or mesh used to write it down, and neither should a surrogate model. Yet today's leading neural surrogates lack these invariances and fail under simple transformations of the same problem: for models trained on PDEs of cars in one pose (i.e., translation and rotation), rotating the full PDE raises the surface-pressure error from 4% to more than 100%, and re-sampling its boundary raises it to about 30%. We introduce ISLA (Invariant Slice Attention), a slice-attention transformer for steady, boundary-driven PDEs. Because the boundary determines the interior solution, ISLA encodes the posed boundary once into learned slices and evaluates arbitrary interior points independently through a tree-accelerated learned boundary kernel. Inputs are nondimensionalized in scales computed from the boundary, sums over boundary cells are area-weighted quadratures that converge under mesh refinement, and geometry enters only as distances and relative angles to equivariant slice anchors, making the model equivariant to rigid motions and reflections up to optional token subsampling and tree clustering. On AeroZoo, 2,816 3D flows spanning diverse geometries, poses, physical scales, and boundary conditions, ISLA's mean reference-scaled velocity and pressure errors are at least 1.9 and 2.2 times lower than any baseline's. On full AirfRANS, ISLA is second only to an explicit boundary-integral network (GLOBE), with errors at least 1.6 times lower than Transolver's and GeoTransolver's in every field.
Computational Engineering.comment: 49 pages, 14 figures, 27 tables. Companion paper to "AeroZoo: A Benchmark of Well-Posed Flow Problems for Foundation Models of Aerodynamics" (Sharpe et al., 2026, arXiv:2611.17152)

Computational Engineering.title: Matching two-dimensional statistics does not certify three-dimensional transport in battery electrodes
Computational Engineering.summary: Three-dimensional battery electrode structures reconstructed from two-dimensional micrographs are routinely used to predict transport, assuming that matching the measured 2D statistics reproduces the relevant 3D properties. We test this premise on X-ray tomograms of three all-solid-state cathodes. With a differentiable conductivity solver, we optimise voxel structures that match the real electrode in phase fractions, boundary density, two- and three-point correlations and lineal-path functions, on all section planes, slab by slab and layer by layer, within measurement noise. Every sample has statistical twins conducting 10-88-fold less than the real electrode, robust to 5^3 majority filtering, whereas the most conductive are at most 3.3-fold above it. The twins rearrange rather than remove material, severing or funnelling through-plane paths. A classifier on 2D sections detects them, as it does current 2D-to-3D generators: the information is in the images but not in the statistics. Matching standard 2D statistics therefore does not certify 3D transport.
Computational Engineering.comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables; includes Supplementary Information

Computational Engineering.title: UncertainGen: Scalable Uncertainty-Aware Representation Learning of DNA Sequences
Computational Engineering.summary: Learning effective representations of DNA sequences is fundamental to genomic data analysis, especially in the presence of high sequence similarity and inter-species DNA sharing. Existing approaches rely on deterministic embeddings, such as k-mer statistics or representations from large language models, which fail to capture the inherent uncertainty in short and ambiguous DNA fragments. We propose UncertainGen, a lightweight probabilistic representation learning framework that embeds DNA sequences as distributions in a latent space. The learned embedding variance captures positional ambiguity, increasing for sequences compatible with multiple genomic clusters. We establish theoretical guarantees on embedding distinguishability, and show that the probabilistic formulation induces a data-adaptive metric that expands the effective representational space. We evaluate UncertainGen in the metagenomic binning task to demonstrate the practical benefits of uncertainty-aware representations. Experiments show that probabilistic embeddings consistently outperform deterministic k-mer and large genome foundation models, while remaining lightweight and efficient.
Computational Engineering.comment: Accepted to the Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

Computational Engineering.title: REFLEX: Reflexive Equilibrium Fixed-point Learning for Endogenous eXchanges
Computational Engineering.summary: In over-the-counter corporate bond markets, dealers compete for client trades by quoting bid and ask prices. Tighter quotes attract more business, but also informed customers more likely to trade ahead of adverse price moves, leaving the dealer holding the risk. As dealers increasingly use machine learning to set quotes, they retrain these models on the trades their own quotes attract, creating a feedback loop in which each model reshapes the market that generates its next training data. The question is therefore not only whether a quoting model performs well, but whether the market it creates stays stable as the model learns from it. Existing performative prediction theory gives a sharp stability condition, yet expresses it through abstract properties of the learning objective a trading desk cannot measure before deployment. We introduce REFLEX, a framework that replaces those unobservable quantities with three measurable features of dealer behavior: how strongly trading volume responds to tighter quotes, how sharply the dealer's objective bends around its optimum, and how quickly informed flow increases as spreads narrow. REFLEX combines these into a single retraining modulus, a pre-deployment stability margin estimated from a desk's own quote and execution history that predicts whether repeated retraining will converge or amplify itself. In simulation, predicted and measured stability agree within 8%, and competing dealers increase instability by 1.74x with two and 3.16x with three, as predicted. Where ordinary retraining becomes unstable at modulus 1.21, a structurally anchored correction converges as blind retraining collapses. Calibrated over 36 years of public market data, stability headroom falls roughly 4.4x for investment grade and 4.3x for high yield from calm to crisis regimes. Ultimately, REFLEX turns an abstract convergence theorem into a market-level safety margin.
Computational Engineering.comment: Published in the Proceedings of the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance (ICAIF 2026), Milan, Italy

Computational Engineering.title: EnKF-C user guide
Computational Engineering.summary: EnKF-C provides a compact generic framework for off-line data assimilation into large-scale layered geophysical models with the ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF). It is coded in C for GNU/Linux platform and can work either in EnKF, ensemble optimal interpolation (EnOI), or hybrid (EnKF/EnOI) modes.

Computational Engineering.title: PopulationBalanceModels.jl: An Extensible Framework for Deploying Population Balance Models
Computational Engineering.summary: Population balance models (PBMs) are used to describe a diverse range of processes that have a distribution over one or more intrinsic properties. However, implementing PBMs for a new application often requires developing and verifying application-specific code for numerical solution and analysis. In this work, we present PopulationBalanceModels.jl, an open-source Julia package designed to make PBMs easy to implement. Users construct models from individual physical terms and select the numerical methods separately. Common solver and observation interfaces allow the same model to be used for simulation, Bayesian parameter estimation, and uncertainty quantification. The package currently supports various model types such as coupled and/or multi-dimensional PBMs, coupling of a PBM to a bulk mass/energy balance, and transport in an axially-dispersed plug flow reactor. While a broad range of physical terms and corresponding numerical methods are already implemented, the package is designed to support extensibility in both aspects, enabling users to incorporate new mechanisms and numerical methods into existing workflows.
Computational Engineering.comment: 26 pages, 4 figures

Computational Engineering.title: Herding or Racing? Decomposing Cross-Account Order-Flow Persistence in On-Chain Markets
Computational Engineering.summary: Most of the autocorrelation in trade signs on decentralized exchanges comes from pairs of trades sent by different wallets. For Uniswap v3, this has been read as herding dominating order splitting -- the reverse of what equity markets show. We show that this herding share mixes two quantities: the probability $p$ that consecutive orders come from the same account, which is small when thousands of wallets are trading, and the ratio $κ$ of cross-account to same-account sign correlation. For any $p$, $κ$ equals one under the public-signal benchmark of Tóth et al. and zero under independent order splitting. On Uniswap v3 USDC-WETH (one week each in 2023 and 2024), the herding share is 0.65-0.86, but $κ$ is only 0.05-0.10. On a fully on-chain EVM limit order book, the herding share is similar (0.61-0.87), but $κ$ is 0.72-0.76; among Uniswap swaps above USD 100k, it is 0.34-0.52. Where $κ$ is high, cross-account co-movement is mostly a race for the price on a centralized exchange. It is concentrated in orders a few blocks apart, and a cross-fitted gradient-boosted filter that sees only Binance data removes about three quarters or more of it. This race flow accounts for most of the losses of liquidity providers. We recommend reporting $κ$ alongside the herding share and modeling on-chain order flow as splitting traders plus arbitrageurs who respond to the centralized-exchange price.
Computational Engineering.comment: N pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the workshop "AI-Driven Market Microstructure in Centralized and Decentralized Finance" at the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance (ICAIF '26), Milan, November 2026

Computational Engineering.title: Simulated Annealing with Topological Spatial Chunking for De Novo Protein Sequence Design
Computational Engineering.summary: The inverse protein folding problem, designing a discrete amino acid sequence that spontaneously folds into a predefined macroscopic structure, remains a phenomenally demanding combinatorial challenge central to synthetic drug discovery. While algorithms like SA offer a baseline approach for navigating dense biomolecular energy landscapes, applying SA heuristics to large sequences is inherently frustrated by exponentially large search spaces and deep local energy minima. This study proposes a scalable sequence design architecture, Topological Spatial Chunking Simulated Annealing, based on a localized, exact-solving heuristic embedded within a global simulated-annealing wrapper. To fundamentally circumvent exponential scaling walls, we deploy a dynamic solver that segments the global molecular target into shallow, k-variable algorithmic windows. Crucially, rather than partitioning natively by sequential 1D chronology, we introduce topological spatial chunking, which dynamically groups discrete variables based on Euclidean spatial proximity to preserve critical non-local thermodynamic correlations. The spatially localized sub-problems are solved deterministically via exact enumeration, while the global traversal is securely regulated by an exterior simulated annealing governor augmented by dynamic reheating and continuous elitism caching. We comprehensively benchmarked this classical architecture on the standard HP biophysical lattice against targeted 20-merA, 25-mer, 50-mer, and 64-mer geometries. Most notably, when evaluating the computationally exhaustive 50-mer and 64-mer topologies, the framework successfully bypassed widely accepted heuristic boundaries. By leveraging deterministic exact solving to vault classical energy traps, the system algorithmically resolved a novel, ultra-dense sequence-packing configuration for the 50-mer, defining a new theoretical global optimum.

Computational Engineering.title: A predictive, per-engine energy roofline of the Apple Neural Engine
Computational Engineering.summary: The Apple Neural Engine (ANE) is in over a billion devices, but is characterized indirectly via CoreML. Using a CoreML-free fused-graph dispatch path, we measure the ANE, along with the Apple GPU and CPU on the same device, with per-engine energy accounting. The consumer-available roofline does not predict the ANE in practice. A critical correction is that the ANE sees two effective memory bandwidths: a slow activation path and a fast weight-stream path. Two roofline ridges follow, and the weight-stream ridge is below that of the GPU. The ANE single-operand compute peak decreases instead of plateauing. Its weight stream is byte-bound in fp16 but limited by the dequantizer's element rate in int8. As a result, int8 compression saves energy at unchanged throughput and an int4 lookup-table stream raises throughput and efficiency at a cost of 2.55 points of ImageNet top-1. The corrected roofline identifies the lower-energy ANE paths and bounds it from below. A constructed device map reproduces across four unique ANE generations. Results show that operators should be placed by arithmetic intensity and fused for optimal performance.
Computational Engineering.comment: 40 pages, 5 figures, 36 tables (including a 28-table supplement as appendices). Accepted to ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization (TACO). Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24210581

Computational Engineering.title: A Multigrid Finite State Projection Algorithm For The Solution Of The Reaction-Diffusion Master Equation
Computational Engineering.summary: We develop a multigrid method for the direct solution of the reaction-diffusion master equation (RDME). The RDME describes stochastic chemical dynamics through reactions in well-mixed spatial cells, called voxels, and diffusion between them. Its unknowns are probabilities of molecular count configurations, and the growth of this state space is the main computational challenge. Grouping neighboring voxels and summing their counts gives smaller equations down to a chemical master equation on one voxel. Restriction sums residual entries with the same coarse counts, and prolongation distributes corrections by multinomial weights. We derive coarse reaction and diffusion rates and, for reversible diffusion, bound the error omitted by coarsening through graph energy, with a constant independent of population for fixed aggregates and rates. Tests with standard multigrid cycles and Gauss-Seidel smoothing examine spatial and population refinement, reaching 7.16 million states and resolving probabilities of order 1e-7.

Machine Learning.title: Ambient LLMs: Data-Efficient Supervised Fine-tuning via Temperature Matching
Machine Learning.summary: Collecting large-scale, diverse, and high-quality post-training datasets for autoregressive language models is challenging. Consequently, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is typically applied to datasets significantly smaller than those used for pre-training, which leads to overfitting and the catastrophic forgetting of the tails of the data distribution. To prevent this collapse, we introduce Ambient SFT, a principled framework for leveraging imperfect predictions to augment the fine-tuning set. In our method, a "frozen" version of the pre-trained model serves as a noisy teacher that the fine-tuned model must match at a coarse level. In particular, we require that the high-temperature versions of the conditional distributions produced by the post-training model should match the high-temperature versions of the pre-training ones. The temperature hyperparameter controls the level of trust in the pre-trained model, with the limit $T\to \infty$ reverting back to regular SFT and $T=1$ to knowledge distillation. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms standard SFT across domain adaptation, instruction-tuning, and reasoning, leading for up to $21\%$ average relative improvement to standard SFT.

Machine Learning.title: Spool: Low-Latency Streaming Inference for Hybrid Vision-Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: Applications such as visual accessibility agents and robotics require answering questions about recent video content promptly, over a bounded window of past frames (e.g., the last two minutes). Hybrid vision-language models (VLMs), which interleave attention with linear recurrent layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), are attractive for this setting, but maintaining a sliding window is expensive. The reason is that recurrent layers combine all past frames into a shared state, so expiring old frames normally requires re-running the entire window through the model. We observe that the recurrent update is affine in the state with input-dependent coefficients, so the effect of each frame can be captured as a transformation that composes associatively. We present Spool, a training-free framework that caches per-frame state transformations and composes them efficiently as the window advances, removing expired frames from each recurrent layer's state without replaying frames through the backbone. Removal is exact within each layer; as with key-value eviction in attention, expired frames can retain residual influence through the cached inputs computed by earlier layers. We design a dedicated data structure and GPU kernels to achieve low caching and composition overhead. Across five open-source hybrid VLMs and four video reasoning benchmarks, Spool achieves the lowest p95 time-to-first-token in all 20 model-benchmark tests, reducing it by a geometric mean of $6.6\times$ over the faster of two recent vLLM baselines, while improving accuracy by 2.3 percentage points on average.

Machine Learning.title: An inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient method for constrained convex finite-sum optimization
Machine Learning.summary: In this paper, we study a class of constrained convex finite-sum optimization problems. In many practical applications, all or some of the constraints are hard constraints that represent imperative requirements. Consequently, any desirable approximate solution must (nearly) satisfy these constraints. Motivated by this, we focus on computing an $ε$-$surely\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ ($ε$-SFSO) solution, in which the constraint violation is deterministically bounded by $ε$, and the expected optimality gap is at most $ε$. While a recently proposed stochastic variance-reduced first-order penalty method can compute an $ε$-SFSO solution, there remains a significant gap between its first-order oracle complexity for computing an $ε$-SFSO solution and that for computing an $ε$-$expected\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ solution, where both the expected constraint violation and the expected optimality gap are bounded by $ε$. To narrow this gap, we propose an inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient (SVRG) method that significantly improves the previously best-known first-order oracle complexity for computing an $ε$-SFSO solution. Furthermore, when the objective consists of a single function, the proposed method reduces to a novel deterministic first-order method for solving standard convex conic optimization.
